prompt: Experiment 2 differed from Experiment 1 in which of the following ways?

choices.text: The time the lamp had been on was held constant in Experiment 2 but varied in Experiment 1
choices.rationale: Both experiments tested the same set of values of time.

choices.text: The temperature of the room was 20°C in Experiment 1 and 0°C in Experiment 2
choices.rationale: Correct. The description of Experiment 2 says the procedure was repeated with only this condition changed.

choices.text: The lamp used was varied in Experiment 2 but held constant in Experiment 1
choices.rationale: The lamp used was kept the same in both experiments; only the temperature of the room changed.

choices.text: A different quantity was measured in Experiment 2 in place of the voltage of the battery
choices.rationale: Both experiments measured the voltage of the battery.

explanation: Experiment 2 repeated Experiment 1 in a cold room at 0°C; everything else, including the values of time and the quantity measured, stayed the same.

table.caption: Experiment 1: Students connected a fresh AA battery to a small lamp in a room at 20°C and measured the battery's voltage with a voltmeter at regular intervals while the lamp stayed on. Experiment 2: The procedure was repeated in a cold room at 0°C, with everything else unchanged. Table 1 lists the results of both experiments.

prompt: Which of the following hypotheses is best supported by the results of Experiment 1?

choices.text: Soil eroded is greatest at an intermediate slope angle and lower at both higher and lower values.
choices.rationale: The results never reverse direction, so there is no intermediate maximum.

choices.text: Increasing slope angle increases soil eroded.
choices.rationale: Correct. Every increase in the independent variable produced a larger measured value.

choices.text: Increasing slope angle decreases soil eroded.
choices.rationale: The results do not fall with every increase in the independent variable.

choices.text: Slope angle has no effect on soil eroded.
choices.rationale: The measured values change clearly from trial to trial, so there is an effect.

explanation: Reading the results in order of slope angle, the mass of soil eroded increased, which supports: "Increasing slope angle increases soil eroded."

stimulus.title: Slope and Soil Erosion
stimulus.text:
Experiment 1
Students filled identical trays with 5 kg of the same soil, tilted each tray to a set angle, and sprinkled water evenly over it from a watering can. They collected the soil that washed out of the tray, dried it, and found its mass.
Results (the mass of soil eroded): at 5°, 49 g; at 10°, 119 g; at 15°, 209 g; at 20°, 320 g; at 25°, 451 g; at 30°, 603 g.

prompt: In Experiment 1, the experimenters repeated each measurement several times and recorded the average. The most likely reason was to:

choices.text: Make the number of colonies change more in response to antibiotic concentration
choices.rationale: Repeating a measurement cannot change the size of the real effect.

choices.text: Remove the need to keep the volume of culture spread on each plate the same
choices.rationale: Repetition does not substitute for controlling variables; controls are still needed.

choices.text: Increase the range of antibiotic concentration that could be tested
choices.rationale: Repeating a measurement does not change which values of antibiotic concentration are tested.

choices.text: Reduce the effect of random error in individual measurements
choices.rationale: Correct. Averaging repeated measurements cancels out much of the random variation in any single measurement.

explanation: Any single measurement contains random error; repeating and averaging makes the recorded value more reliable.

stimulus.title: Antibiotic Dose and Bacterial Growth
stimulus.text:
Experiment 1
Students spread 0.1 mL of a bacterial culture onto agar plates containing a known concentration of an antibiotic. After 24 hours they counted the colonies on each plate. Three plates were prepared for each concentration and the average count was recorded.
Results (the number of colonies): at 5 µg/mL, 107 colonies; at 10 µg/mL, 41 colonies; at 15 µg/mL, 16 colonies; at 20 µg/mL, 6 colonies; at 25 µg/mL, 2 colonies.

prompt: Suppose the experimenters had run one more trial in Experiment 1 at a light intensity of 150 µmol/m²/s. Based on the results, the rate of photosynthesis in that trial would most likely have been:

choices.text: below every result obtained, less than 18.5 bubbles/min
choices.rationale: This is below every result; the trend gives no reason to expect it.

choices.text: between 18.5 bubbles/min and 24.9 bubbles/min
choices.rationale: Correct. 150 µmol/m²/s is between the tested values 100 µmol/m²/s and 200 µmol/m²/s, whose results were 18.5 and 24.9.

choices.text: between 24.9 bubbles/min and 28.2 bubbles/min
choices.rationale: This interval belongs to light intensity between 200 µmol/m²/s and 300 µmol/m²/s.

choices.text: above every result obtained, greater than 32.4 bubbles/min
choices.rationale: This is above every result; the trend gives no reason to expect it.

explanation: The results change steadily with light intensity, so a trial at 150 µmol/m²/s should give a value between those of its neighbors, 18.5 and 24.9 bubbles/min.

stimulus.title: Light and Photosynthesis
stimulus.text:
Experiment 1
Students placed a sprig of pondweed in a test tube of water and set a lamp at distances giving several light intensities. They counted the oxygen bubbles released in one minute at each intensity, repeating each count three times.
Results (the rate of photosynthesis): at 100 µmol/m²/s, 18.5 bubbles/min; at 200 µmol/m²/s, 24.9 bubbles/min; at 300 µmol/m²/s, 28.2 bubbles/min; at 400 µmol/m²/s, 30.1 bubbles/min; at 500 µmol/m²/s, 31.5 bubbles/min; at 600 µmol/m²/s, 32.4 bubbles/min.

The cup sat on a table in a room at a constant temperature. Experiment 2: The procedure was repeated using an insulated foam cup, with everything else unchanged. prompt: Based on Experiment 1, which conclusion is best supported?

choices.text: Increasing depth decreases temperature.
choices.rationale: Correct. Every increase in the independent variable produced a smaller measured value.

choices.text: Increasing depth increases temperature.
choices.rationale: The results do not rise with every increase in the independent variable.

choices.text: Temperature is greatest at an intermediate depth and lower at both higher and lower values.
choices.rationale: The results never reverse direction, so there is no intermediate maximum.

choices.text: The location of the boat determines temperature.
choices.rationale: The location of the boat was held constant, so the experiment says nothing about its effect.

explanation: Reading the results in order of depth, the water temperature decreased, which supports: "Increasing depth decreases temperature."

stimulus.title: Lake Temperature and Depth
stimulus.text:
Experiment 1
From a boat anchored over the deepest part of a lake, students lowered a thermometer probe on a marked cable and recorded the water temperature at several depths. All readings were taken within one hour at midday.
Results (the water temperature): at 0 m, 25.3 °C; at 2 m, 16.1 °C; at 4 m, 11.3 °C; at 6 m, 8.8 °C; at 8 m, 7.5 °C.

stimulus.title: Fertilizer and Plant Growth
stimulus.text:
Experiment 1
Students planted bean seeds in identical pots of potting soil and watered each pot with 100 mL of fertilizer solution every other day. After 4 weeks they measured the height of each seedling. Each concentration was tested with five pots, and the average height was recorded.
Results (the height of the seedlings): at 5 g/L, 20.0 cm; at 10 g/L, 22.9 cm; at 15 g/L, 23.1 cm; at 20 g/L, 20.8 cm; at 25 g/L, 15.8 cm.

stimulus.title: Catalyst and Reaction Time
stimulus.text:
Experiment 1
Students mixed 50 mL of hydrogen peroxide solution from a single bottle with a measured mass of powdered catalyst and timed how long it took for the bubbling to stop.
Results (the time for the reaction to finish): at 0 mg, 221 s; at 2 mg, 128 s; at 4 mg, 77 s; at 6 mg, 49 s; at 8 mg, 33 s; at 10 mg, 25 s.

stimulus.title: Insulation and Heat Loss
stimulus.text:
Experiment 1
Students wrapped a metal box containing an electric heater in foam sheets of a set total thickness. They adjusted the heater power until the inside temperature held steady in a 20°C room and recorded that power as the rate of heat loss.
Results (the rate of heat loss): at 0 cm, 143 W; at 2 cm, 88 W; at 4 cm, 64 W; at 6 cm, 50 W; at 8 cm, 41 W.

stimulus.title: Enzyme Activity and pH
stimulus.text:
Experiment 1
Students added 1 mL of enzyme solution to tubes containing a substrate solution buffered to a set pH. They measured how much product formed in 5 minutes to find the activity. Each pH was tested in triplicate.
Results (the activity of the enzyme): at pH 4, 20 µmol/min; at pH 5, 44 µmol/min; at pH 6, 63 µmol/min; at pH 7, 58 µmol/min; at pH 8, 34 µmol/min.
